'''Chikatō Kami''' (千鹿頭神, Chikatō Kami or Chikatou-no-Kami) is a {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto}} deity ({{ill|Folk religion|en|Folk religion|qid=Q1068640|lt=folk belief}}) primarily worshiped in {{ill|Nagano == Overview ==
[[File:Moriya Family Tree - 守矢氏系図.png|thumb|345x345px|Family tree of the {{ill|Moriya clan|ja|守矢氏|en|Moriya clan}} according to 『Shuya Clan Genealogy』 showing the first five generations (from Moriya to Hachikushi Kami)]]
In the folk traditions of the {{ill|Suwa Region|ja|諏訪地方|en|Suwa Region|lt=Suwa region}} ({{ill|Suwa Shrine|ja|諏訪信仰|en|Suwa Shrine|lt=Suwa faith}}), Chikatō Kami is considered the offspring deity of {{ill|Moreya|en|Moreya|qid=Q11146526|lt=Moriya}} and his descendants, or alternatively, an alias of that deity. Chikatō Kami is sometimes equated with {{ill|Takeminakata|en|Takeminakata|qid=Q9150391|qid=Q9150391|lt=Takeminakata's}} offspring deity {{nihongo|Uchi Prefecture Kami|内県神|en|lt=Uchi Prefecture Kami}}.
According to the 『Shuya Clan Genealogy』, Chikatō Kami is the son of {{ill|Mote Takami|ja|洩宅神|en|Mote Takami|lt=Moritaku-no-Kami}}, the son of {{ill|Moreya|en|Moreya|qid=Q11146526|lt=Moriya-no-Kami}}, and is counted as the third generation of the {{ill|Moriya clan|ja|守矢氏|en|Moriya clan|lt=Moriya clan}}. His name originates from an event where his father, while hunting, captured 1,000 deer, hence the name "Chikatō" (千鹿頭, meaning "thousand deer head").
<blockquote>Chikatō Kami was born with extraordinary spiritual powers, taking over hunting duties from his father, and followed the Great Deity in hunting and game. He obtained a thousand deer. He had one son, whom he named Chikatō Kami.
Chikatō Kami succeeded his father in overseeing ceremonial affairs.</blockquote>
Ancient {{ill|Kagura|ja|kagura|en|Kagura}} songs:
:Chikatō no Kitano Hayashinowa Susumushiwa Susumushiwa Yachiyo no Koyete Tsunenitaisenu
:Chikatō no Myōjin Shiyushūreshito Ohosoransu Ohosoransu Yukitataima no Hana no Kiyomeyo
Chikatō's shrines are located in {{ill|Suwa District, Nagano|en|Suwa District, Nagano|qid=Q1131473|lt=Suwa District}} in Aruga, Uehara, Hanahara, Yokobuki, Kyudo, {{ill|Higashichikuma District, Nagano|en|Higashichikuma District, Nagano|qid=Q1155105|lt=Higashichikuma District}} Kanda, Hayashi both located in {{ill|Iida|ja|Iida|en|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11224660}} District, {{ill|Fukushima District, Fukushima|ja|Fukushima|en|Fukushima District, Fukushima}} Prefecture, and in {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|en|Yamanashi Prefecture|qid=Q132720|lt=Toyama Prefecture}} and {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}} among others. In the area {{ill|Urakoyama|ja|宇良古山|en|Urakoyama|lt=Urakoyama}} is situated, there exists a shrine dedicated to him.
{{ill|Kodama Hiko-no-Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命|en|Kodama Hiko-no-Mikoto|lt=Kodamahiko-no-Mikoto}}, the offspring of the Great Deity's child {{ill|Kataura Hade-no-Mikoto|ja|片倉辺命|en|Kataura Hade-no-Mikoto|lt=Katakurabe no Mikoto}}, is considered the successor of Chikatō Kami. He married {{ill|Mitasama Hime-no-Kami|ja|美都多麻比売神|en|Mitasama Hime-no-Kami|lt=Mitasama Hime-no-Kami}}, the child of {{ill|Moritachi no Kami|ja|守達神|en|Moritachi no Kami|lt=Moritatsu-no-Kami}}, and gave birth to {{ill|Hachikushi|ja|八櫛神|en|Hachikushi|lt=Hachikushi}}.<ref name="Moriyakeifu">Suwa Education Association. "『Shuya Clan Genealogy』" 『Suwa Historical Documents Collection, Volume 28』, 1938, pp. 31-72.</ref><ref name="nomotochikato">Nomoto Mikato. "Approach to Chikatō Kami" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 333-336.</ref><ref name="imaidd7">Imai Nohiku. "O Suwa-sama Faith and Kami no Naga" 『Gods' Village: Ancient Suwa Stories』, Kokusho Publishing, 1976, pp. dd7-dd8.</ref>
According to the 『Genealogy』, Chikatō Kami married {{ill|Uragokohime-no-Mikoto|ja|宇良古比売命|en|Uragokohime-no-Mikoto|lt=Uragokohime-no-Mikoto}} and moved to {{ill|Urakoyama|ja|宇良古山|en|Urakoyama|lt=Urakoyama}} (now {{ill|Matsumoto, Nagano|ar|ماتسوموتو (ناغانو)|az|Matsumoto|azb|ماتسوموتو، ناقانو|bg|Мацумото|ca|Matsumoto (ciutat)|ce|Мацумото (гӀала)|ceb|Matsumoto (lungsod sa Hapon)|ckb|ماتسومۆتۆ، ناگانۆ|cs|Macumoto|da|Matsumoto|de|Matsumoto|eo|Macumoto (Nagano)|es|Matsumoto (Nagano)|et|Matsumoto|eu|Matsumoto (Nagano)|fa|ماتسوموتو، ناگانو|fi|Matsumoto (Nagano)|fr|Matsumoto (Nagano)|ga|Matsumoto|gl|Matsumoto|ha|Matsumoto, Nagano|hy|Մացումոտո (քաղաք)|id|Matsumoto, Nagano|it|Matsumoto|ja|松本市|ko|마쓰모토시|mdf|Мацумота (Нагано)|ms|Matsumoto|mzn|ماتسوموتو، ناگانو|nl|Matsumoto|nn|Matsumoto i Nagano|no|Matsumoto (Nagano)|os|Мацумото (сахар)|pl|Matsumoto|pt|Matsumoto (Nagano)|ro|Matsumoto, Nagano|ru|Мацумото (город)|sh|Matsumoto|simple|Matsumoto, Nagano|sl|Macumoto, Nagano|sr|Мацумото|sv|Matsumoto|tg|Матсумото|th|มัตสึโมโตะ|tl|Matsumoto, Nagano|tr|Matsumoto|tt|Мацумото (шәһәр)|uk|Мацумото (Наґано)|ur|ماتسوموتو، ناگانو|vi|Matsumoto|war|Matsumoto, Nagano|zh|松本市|zh_classical|松本市|zh_min_nan|Matumoto-chhī|zh_yue|松本|qid=Q213324|lt=Matsumoto City}}, {{ill|Shinden (divine field)|ja|神田|en|lt=Kanda|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q10855080}}), which suggests that Chikatō Kami was either exiled from Suwa or left voluntarily. It is also believed that the succession of Chikatō Kami by {{ill|Takeminakata|en|Takeminakata|qid=Q9150391|lt=Take Minakata}}'s grandchild {{ill|Kodamahiko-no-Mikoto|ja|児玉彦命|en|Kodamahiko-no-Mikoto|lt=Kodamahiko-no-Mikoto}} indicates that the {{ill|Suwa clan|en|Suwa clan|qid=Q2975376|lt=Suwa Clan}} (descendants of the mythological {{ill|Takeminakata|en|Takeminakata|qid=Q9150391|lt=Take Minakata}}) took over the local worship duties of indigenous forces.
There are also traditions where the foreign-born Chikatō Kami married local daughters not only in Matsumoto but also in other places. A famous tale narrates that "Chikato Kami" from Shinshu came to {{ill|Akagiyama Shrine|ja|赤城神社|en|Akagiyama Shrine|lt=Akagiyama Shrine}} and married the sister of the {{ill|Akagi Shrines|ja|赤城神|en|Akagi Shrines|lt=Akagi Shrines}}.<ref>Imai Nohiku. "Chikato-sama" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 325.</ref><ref>Nomoto Mikato. "Approach to Chikatō Kami" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 342.</ref>

They have various representations such as "Chikatō," "Chikata," "Chikato," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," "Chikata," and "Chikata," with pronunciations including "Chikata," "Chikatsu," "Chikato (u)," etc.<ref name="imai326">Imai Nohiku. "Chikatō Kami Approach" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 326.</ref><ref>Nomoto Mikato. "Approach to Chikatō Kami" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 343.</ref>
The distribution of Chikatō Kami shrines is characterized by their apparent movement along mountainous regions (such as the {{ill|Yatsugatake|en|Yatsugatake}}, {{ill|Haruna|en|Haruna}}, {{ill|Akagi|en|Akagi}}, {{ill|Mount Ontake|en|Mount Ontake}}, {{ill|Yamigomezaki|en|Yamigomezaki}}) and is believed to have spread through the eastward expansion of hunting clans (descendants of the {{ill|Moriya|ja|Moriya clan|en|Moriya}}). As deities of hunting, they are closely related to {{ill|Mishagujishin|ja|ミシャグジ信仰}} and {{ill|Tenpaku faith|ja|天白信仰|lt=Tenpaku Faith}}. From Imai's research, it is evident that in Yamanashi, Saitama, and Gunma, {{ill|Mishagujishin|ja|ミシャグジ信仰}} shrines coincide with Chikatō Kami shrines.<ref>Yamato Iwao. "Shinano Ancient History Study" 『Shinano Ancient History Study』, Meicho Publishing, 1990, pp. 201-202.</ref><ref>Imai Nohiku. "Survey Collection of Shrine Priests" 『Study on Ancient Suwa and Mishagujis' Ceremonial Systems』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2017, pp. 212-281.</ref>
In addition to hunting deities from Suwa (Shinshu), there are regions where Chikatō Kami is also revered as a deity of agriculture and fire prevention, similar to {{ill|Mishagujishin|ja|ミシャグジ信仰}} and {{ill|Tenpaku faith|ja|天白信仰|lt=Tenpaku Faith}}, with many shrines worshiping them as {{ill|Sekibō|en|Sekibō|qid=Q17994957|lt=Sekibō}} deities.<ref>Nomoto Mikato. "Approach to Chikatō Kami" 『Study on the Emergence and Development of Suwa Faith』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2018, pp. 347-349.</ref><ref>Imai Nohiku. "Survey of Shrine Priests" 『Study on Ancient Suwa and Mishagujis' Ceremonial Systems』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2017, pp. 300-301.</ref><ref>Imai Nohiku. "Survey of Shrine Priests" 『Study on Ancient Suwa and Mishagujis' Ceremonial Systems』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2017, pp. 338-339.</ref><ref>Tanaka Moto. "Primitive Agricultural Ritual Elements in Mote Yashima Ceremonial System" 『Study on Ancient Suwa and Mishagujis' Ceremonial Systems』, Ancient Tribe Research Society edited by Jinkan-sha, 2017, p. 192.</ref>.
